title: Job loses everything (Job 1–2)
hookLine: a good man loses children, wealth and health; his friends first sit silent seven days

lines: A MAN IN THE LAND OF HUS.
DOES JOB FEAR GOD FOR NOTHING?
cards: The book opens like a folk tale, in the Douay-Rheims: "There was a man in the land of Hus, whose name was Job." Simple and upright, fearing God.
Seven sons, three daughters, thousands of sheep and camels, the greatest man in the East.

Then the scene shifts to heaven, where the sons of God come before the Lord, and among them is Satan; the Hebrew says ha-satan, the adversary, with the article, like a title in the court. God points out Job.
The adversary shrugs: does Job fear God for nothing? Take it all away and see.

teach.b: Then the messengers start arriving, each still speaking when the next runs in. Raiders took the oxen. Fire fell and burned the sheep.
Raiders took the camels. And the last: a great wind struck the house where your children were eating, and it fell on them, and they are dead.
Job tears his robe, shaves his head, falls to the ground, and worships: naked I came out of my mother's womb, and naked I shall return.

teach.h: THE LORD GAVE, THE LORD HATH TAKEN.
teach.b: The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord. Then his health goes too, sores from his feet to his head, and he sits on a dunghill scraping himself with a broken piece of pottery.
Three friends hear of it, Eliphaz, Baldad and Sophar, and agree to come together to comfort him. From far off they don't recognize him. They weep aloud, tear their robes, throw dust over their heads.

teach.h: SEVEN DAYS ON THE GROUND, NO WORD.
teach.b: And then the Douay says: "they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no man spoke to him a word: for they saw that his grief was very great." Seven days. No speeches.
In chapter three Job finally speaks, and then the friends start answering, and for chapter after chapter they explain his suffering to him: he must have done something.

teach.h: THEY SAW THAT HIS GRIEF WAS VERY GREAT.
teach.b: At the very end, God says they did not speak rightly about him. So the part Job's friends got right was the first week, on the ground, with their mouths shut.

how: The Church's traditional Office of the Dead draws its readings from Job, and at Catholic wakes visitors come to keep company with the grieving family as much as to speak.

s: Job's friends began by explaining why he was suffering
they sat with him seven days and seven nights and nobody spoke a word.
at the end God says the friends had not spoken rightly
in chapter 42; their explanations were the part they got wrong.
when he loses everything, Job curses God

games.q: you're Eliphaz. you've traveled to comfort your friend, and you find him unrecognizable, sitting on a dunghill scraping his sores. what do you do?
o: explain that God must be punishing something he did.
sit down on the ground with him and say nothing.
pray aloud over him and leave.
games.why: seven days and seven nights, and no man spoke to him a word. the trouble begins later, when they start explaining.

practice: If someone comes to mind whose grief is very great, picture arriving and sitting down on the ground beside them. Notice the urge to say something, a reason, a bright side, a story about your own aunt, and let it pass, and stay.
If you pray, hold that person before God without words.

wordCard.voice: ha-satan. Hebrew for the adversary: the heavenly accuser who challenged God to strip Job of his children, his wealth and his health. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the adversary, with the definite article, a role in the heavenly court in Job 1–2.

carryVoice: Your line: they sat with him. Seven days, and not one word. Day four hundred thirty-one, done.
